content: Nafcillin is an antibiotic commonly used to treat infections caused by specific types of bacteria. However, it is not effective against all infections, as some bacteria may have developed resistance to it. This medication works by preventing bacteria from forming their cell walls, which ultimately kills them. It is important to note that nafcillin is only effective against bacterial infections and will not work for viral infections such as the common cold, influenza, or COVID-19. Using nafcillin or any antibiotic unnecessarily can lead to reduced effectiveness in treating future bacterial infections. Nafcillin is typically administered as an injection into a muscle or vein by a healthcare provider in a hospital or clinical setting. It is available in various dosage forms, including 1 g, 2 g, 10 g, and 20 mg/mL injections. If you are prescribed nafcillin for home use, it is crucial to store it properly, keep it out of reach of children, and avoid sharing it with others, even if they have similar symptoms. Before starting nafcillin, inform your healthcare provider about your medical history, including any allergies to penicillin, other medications, or corn products. Additionally, disclose any history of asthma, liver or kidney disease, or antibiotic-associated diarrhea. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, discuss the potential risks and benefits with your healthcare provider, as nafcillin passes into breast milk. Nafcillin may interact with other medications, such as tetracyclines, warfarin, cyclosporine, and probenecid. Always inform your healthcare provider about all prescription and over-the-counter medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking to avoid potential interactions. Common side effects of nafcillin include pain, swelling, or inflammation at the injection site and rash. Serious side effects, though less common, may include severe allergic reactions, seizures, kidney damage, liver damage, blood disorders, and antibiotic-associated diarrhea caused by Clostridioides difficile overgrowth. If you experience symptoms such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, severe rash, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or persistent diarrhea, seek medical attention immediately. Nafcillin is primarily metabolized and excreted by the liver, with a smaller portion eliminated through the kidneys. Patients with liver or kidney dysfunction should use this medication with caution, as it may increase the risk of adverse effects. Periodic monitoring of liver and kidney function, as well as blood counts, is recommended during prolonged therapy, especially when high doses are used. Skipping doses or stopping treatment early may increase the risk of developing antibiotic-resistant bacteria. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it is almost time for the next dose. Do not double doses to make up for a missed one. In case of an overdose, seek immediate medical attention by calling 911 or contacting a poison control center. Overdose symptoms may require discontinuation of the medication and supportive treatment. Nafcillin should not be used in individuals with known allergies to its ingredients or penicillin. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported and are more likely in individuals with a history of penicillin allergy or sensitivity to multiple allergens. If an allergic reaction occurs, discontinue the medication and initiate appropriate treatment. Lastly, nafcillin should only be prescribed for proven or strongly suspected bacterial infections to minimize the risk of drug-resistant bacteria. Overuse or misuse of antibiotics can lead to reduced effectiveness in treating future infections.
